title: Research: Python AST and syntax for refactoring test coverage
description: Gather and summarize information about Python's AST structure, tricky syntax edge cases, commenting and whitespace rules, name resolution rules, and module dependency patterns relevant to jedi's refactoring operations. Output: a checked-in document at docs/refactor_research.md that other agents can use to find gaps in test coverage.
close_reason: Research complete. Document at docs/refactor_research.md covers: AST assignment variants, operator precedence/parenthesization, comments/whitespace, LEGB edge cases, module/import patterns, async/await, f-strings, type annotations, decorators, special statement forms, and per-refactor gap analysis for all six refactors.

title: Implement Introduce Field refactoring (Core 6)
description: Add introduce_field to jedi's refactoring toolkit. Takes a local variable/expression inside a method and promotes it to an instance field (self.x), updating callers.

title: Implement Introduce Parameter refactoring (Core 6)
description: Add introduce_parameter to jedi's refactoring toolkit. Takes a variable/expression inside a function and promotes it to a parameter, updating all call sites.

title: rename: built-in name shadowed by local variable
description: When a local variable shadows a built-in name (e.g. 'list = []'), renaming the local 'list' to 'lst' should not affect built-in 'list' references in other parts of the file or other files. Add a test in test/refactor/rename.py verifying that only the local binding is renamed.

title: rename: comprehension iterable uses outer var with same name as loop var
description: When an outer variable name matches the comprehension loop variable (e.g. 'items = [1,2,3]; result = [item for item in items]'), renaming outer 'items' should update only 'items' in the iterable position, not the loop variable 'item'. This is a different case from comprehension-scope. Add a test in test/refactor/rename.py.

title: rename: except-as var that shadows an outer-scope name
description: In Python 3, 'except E as x' deletes 'x' after the except block (PEP 3110). If 'x' also exists in the outer scope, rename of the except-as binding should only rename within the except block, not the outer 'x'. The current except-as-var test covers simple renaming but not the case where the except variable shadows an outer name. Add a test to test/refactor/rename.py.

title: rename: module var chased through global decl in deeply nested function
description: When a module-level variable is declared 'global x' inside a doubly-nested function (global in g inside f), renaming the module-level x should follow through the 'global x' declaration in the nested function. The current global-decl test uses a single-level nesting. Add a test with x=0 / def f: def g: global x; x=1. to test/refactor/rename.py.

title: rename: nonlocal shared by sibling closures (writer + reader)
description: When two sibling functions both close over the same enclosing variable, and one uses 'nonlocal x', renaming 'x' inside the writer should also rename the usage in the reader and the outer definition. The current nonlocal-rename test only covers a single inner function. Add a test with outer/writer/reader pattern to test/refactor/rename.py.

title: rename: module-level name used at class body level (not in method)
description: Rename of a module-level name that is referenced directly in a class body (not inside any method, e.g. class-level attribute using the module var: 'class Foo: bar = module_var + 1') should correctly find and update the reference. Class bodies do not close over enclosing scope the same way functions do. Add a test in test/refactor/rename.py.

title: rename: property renames both @property def and @x.setter def
description: Renaming a property 'x' in a class should rename both 'def x' under @property and 'def x' under @x.setter, as well as updating '@x.setter' to '@new_name.setter'. No test currently covers this. Add a test in test/refactor/rename.py.

title: rename: f-string format-spec variable (f"{v:{width}}")
description: When a variable appears in the format-spec sub-expression of an f-string (e.g. f"{value:{width}}"), renaming 'width' should update the reference inside the format spec. The existing fstring-var test only covers the value expression. Add a test case in test/refactor/rename.py.

title: introduce_parameter: **kwargs in signature would create syntax error
description: When the last parameter is **kwargs, appending 'x=1' after it produces 'def f(**kwargs, x=1):' which is a SyntaxError (params cannot follow **kwargs). The implementation does not guard against this. Add test 'star-star-kwargs-error' and fix the implementation to raise a RefactoringError.

title: rename: f-string debug specifier (f"{value=}")
description: Python 3.8+ supports f"{value=}" which shows the variable name and its value. Renaming 'value' should produce f"{renamed_value=}". The existing fstring-var test does not cover the '=' debug specifier. Add a test case in test/refactor/rename.py.

title: rename: augmented assignment target (x += 1)
description: No test for rename when the cursor is on a variable that is the target of an augmented assignment (x += 1). The rename should update all occurrences. Add test in test/refactor/rename.py.

title: rename: annotated declaration without value (x: int)
description: An annotated assignment without a value (x: int) is a valid name binding. Renaming 'x' should work (unlike inline which should error). No test for this. Add a test case in test/refactor/rename.py with 'x: int' and a usage, verify the rename propagates correctly.

title: rename: star-unpacking target (a, *b, c = seq)
description: No test for rename when cursor is on a starred target 'b' in 'a, *b, c = seq' or on a/c. The rename should correctly identify the binding and rename all uses of 'b' (the starred variable). Add test in test/refactor/rename.py.

title: rename: multiple-assignment target (a = b = 1)
description: When cursor is on 'a' in 'a = b = 1', both 'a' and 'b' may refer to the same value but are separate bindings. Or more precisely: renaming 'a' should only rename 'a'. No test currently covers multiple-assignment-target scenarios. Add test in test/refactor/rename.py.

title: rename: self/cls rename across all methods of class
description: Renaming the first parameter of methods (self → this, or cls → klass) is valid Python but there is no test for it. The nonconventional-self-param introduce_field test uses 'this', but rename itself is not tested. Add a test in test/refactor/rename.py that renames 'self' across two methods of a class.

title: rename: __all__ list update when renaming exported name
description: When a module-level name appears in __all__ as a string (e.g. __all__ = ['foo', 'bar']), renaming 'foo' should also update the string literal 'foo' in __all__. No test currently covers this. Add a test case to test/refactor/rename.py with a module-level function in __all__ and verify the rename propagates into the list.

title: review 99f81bf3: introduce.py duplicates helpers from refactoring/__init__.py
description:
Commit 99f81bf3 (Add introduce_parameter and introduce_field) added jedi/api/refactoring/introduce.py with two issues:

1. _remove_indent_of_prefix() at line 275 of introduce.py is a verbatim copy of _remove_indent_of_prefix() in jedi/api/refactoring/__init__.py (line 277). The function should be imported from __init__.py instead.

2. _rename_references() and _replace_references_with_field() are structurally identical tree-walking functions that differ only in the action taken on a matched name node. The shared skeleton (try/except AttributeError, guard for funcdef/classdef/trailer-dot) should be factored into a single walk helper that accepts a callback, or the two functions should be unified.

Neither issue affects correctness, but both create maintenance burden: a bug fix in the shared logic must be applied in two (or three) places.

title: review 48c37298: _is_safe_without_parens uses type-name heuristics, not precedence
description:
Commit 48c37298 (fix inline adding unnecessary parens) introduced _is_safe_without_parens() which checks a hardcoded list of node type names:

    if rhs.type in ('number', 'string', 'keyword', 'fstring'):
        return True
    if rhs.type == 'name':
        return True
    if rhs.type == 'atom' and hasattr(rhs, 'children') and rhs.children:
        first_child = rhs.children[0]
        if hasattr(first_child, 'value') and first_child.value in ('(', '[', '{'):
            return True
    return False

This approach has two problems:

1. It is a heuristic: it enumerates safe cases rather than reasoning from the AST structure. Whether parens are needed depends on the *context* (what expression the inlined value appears in) and the *precedence* of the inlined expression, not just whether the expression is a simple atom. The existing 'needs_parens' logic already captures the context; what's missing is a proper precedence comparison.

2. It uses hasattr() for duck-typing rather than parso's BaseNode/Leaf distinction or isinstance checks. Parso nodes always have .children (non-leaf) or .value (leaf) — defensive hasattr checks obscure this.

The fix should either: (a) extend the type-name list more carefully with tests for each added type, or (b) replace the heuristic with a precedence table keyed on node types (the principled approach). At minimum, add tests for cases not yet covered: unary expressions (x = -1), attribute access (x = a.b), subscript (x = a[0]).

title: review 3b431cf3+6030d2c9: _FRIENDLY_TYPE_NAMES fstring_start is dead code
description:
Commits 3b431cf3 (error message improvements) and 6030d2c9 (f-string extraction fix) were applied in sequence, leaving dead code.

3b431cf3 added _FRIENDLY_TYPE_NAMES = {'fstring_start': 'f-string', ...} to produce a better error message when the user tries to extract an fstring_start node.

6030d2c9 then added fstring_start to _is_not_extractable_syntax(), which causes cursor-climbing to the parent fstring node before _is_expression_with_error() is ever called. So the error path that would use _FRIENDLY_TYPE_NAMES['fstring_start'] is now unreachable — the node will have been promoted to 'fstring' (which IS in _VARIABLE_EXCTRACTABLE) before the check runs.

Additionally: there is no longer an error test for attempting to extract a sub-expression inside an f-string (e.g., extracting 'a' from 'f"val={a}"'). The old fstring-error test was removed by 6030d2c9 and not replaced. Add a test for this case and clarify what the expected behavior is (error or a different kind of climbing).

title: review d531a55b: _contains_await has dead await_expr branch
description:
Commit d531a55b (Fix extract_function for async) introduced _contains_await() in jedi/api/refactoring/extract.py. The function has a dead branch:

    else:
        if node.type == 'await_expr':   # dead code
            return True

Parso does NOT use an 'await_expr' node type. 'await x()' is parsed as atom_expr([<Keyword: await>, <Name: x>, <trailer: ()>]). The 'await' keyword is a leaf node, so it is found via the 'except AttributeError' branch. The 'await_expr' check in the else branch is unreachable.

The function works correctly despite the dead code, but the dead branch creates confusion about parso's AST structure. Fix: remove the dead 'await_expr' branch and add a comment explaining that parso represents 'await expr' as an atom_expr whose first child is a keyword leaf with value 'await'.

Also: no test for extracting code that contains a bare 'await' keyword without a call (e.g. 'await fut'), or for async generators.

title: introduce_field: add test confirming first-param name used for self
description:
Comment on commit 99f81bf: 'How do we determine whether it has a self parameter? Hopefully we are not just looking for a parameter named "self"?'

The code uses params[0].name.value — the name of the first parameter, whatever it is. The existing cls-param test already covers 'cls'. The code is correct.

Action: add a test using a non-conventional first parameter name (e.g. 'this') to further document that any first-parameter name is supported, not just 'self' or 'cls'.

title: introduce_parameter: document call-site behavior
description:
Comment on commit 99f81bf: 'I've noticed all of these tests are only checking the local function. What happens at the call site? Is it always possible to omit the new parameter?'

Since introduce_parameter always adds a default value (the original RHS), all existing call sites remain valid without modification — callers can omit the new parameter and the default will be used. This is correct and intentional design behavior.

Action: add a test case that includes a call site, verifying it is unchanged after the refactoring, to document that this is expected.

title: introduce_field/parameter: fix _find_enclosing_funcdef crossing class boundaries
description:
Comment on commit 99f81bf: 'Aren't there other types of constructs that could interfere with the binding of the name to the function? For example:
    def a():
        class Foo:
            b=7
b is a class attribute of Foo, not a local variable in a().'

Bug: _find_enclosing_funcdef traverses upward through classdef nodes. If a variable is defined inside a nested class (e.g. Foo.b), the function incorrectly returns the outer method (a), causing introduce_parameter to add 'b' as a parameter of 'a' and remove it from Foo's body.

Fix: make _find_enclosing_funcdef return None when it encounters a classdef before finding a funcdef. Add nested-class-var-error tests to both introduce_field.py and introduce_parameter.py.

title: introduce_parameter: reject call expressions as default values
description:
Comment on commit 99f81bf: 'This is also a bug. In the original function, bar() would be called on every invocation. In the new function, bar() gets called during function definition and then never again.'

introduce_parameter currently accepts call expressions (e.g. x = bar()) as defaults, producing semantically different code. bar() would be evaluated once at function definition time instead of each call.

Fix: raise RefactoringError when the RHS is a call expression (atom_expr with a call trailer). Change test case call-default from 'text' to 'error' expectation.

title: introduce_parameter: reject mutable default values
description:
Comments on commit 99f81bf:
- 'This is a bug. A parameter default that is not a primitive will retain its identity from one function call to the next. If foo() appended to the item list, for example, then the next call to foo() would see that larger list.'
- 'Obviously only an issue if the default is mutable.'

introduce_parameter currently accepts mutable literals (lists, dicts, sets) as defaults, producing semantically different code. A parameter default of [1,2,3] shares the same list across all calls, whereas the original local variable created a fresh list each time.

Fix: raise RefactoringError for mutable literal defaults (atom nodes with '[' or '{' as first child). Change test cases list-default and dict-default from 'text' to 'error' expectations.

title: introduce_field: remove redundant type-value tests
description:
Comment on commit 99f81bf: 'Are these <type>-value tests interesting? Aren't they just all opaque expressions, as far as the refactoring code is concerned?'

The tests string-value, expression-value, list-value, none-value, dict-value, bool-value in test/refactor/introduce_field.py don't test anything different from 'simple'. The refactoring code treats the RHS as an opaque string regardless of type. Remove these redundant tests.

title: introduce_field: error when field already exists
description:
Comment on commit 99f81bf: 'What if there is already a field named x?'

If self.x already exists in the method, introduce_field should raise an error rather than introducing a conflicting second assignment.

Implement: check for existing self.{var_name} references in the function body before proceeding. Add test 'field-already-exists-error' to test/refactor/introduce_field.py.

title: extract_function from async body produces non-async function
description: When extracting an expression containing await from an async function, the extracted function is created as a regular def (not async def) and the call site omits await. The extracted code will fail at runtime since await is used outside async context. Rope handles this by making the extracted function async.
close_reason: Fixed: extract_function now produces async def and await calls when extracting code with await expressions

title: rename with nonlocal doesn't update nonlocal declaration or outer scope
description: When renaming a variable that has a nonlocal declaration, jedi renames the assignment and local uses but does NOT update: (1) the nonlocal x declaration itself, (2) references in the outer scope (e.g., return x). This produces broken code. Discovered during probe testing. Rope handles this correctly.

title: Add untested literal and syntax tests
description: Several literal types untested: set literals, bytes, multiline strings, raw strings, ellipsis, complex numbers. Also: with multiple context managers, for-else, while loop, assert, raise, del.
close_reason: Added set/bytes/ellipsis/raw-string/generator tests and for-loop/with-as rename tests

title: Add import-as aliasing tests
description: import x as y and from x import y as z are untested in all operations. Rename should update the alias and all references. Inline involving aliased imports needs testing.

title: Add walrus operator tests beyond error cases
description: Walrus operator currently only tested as error in extract_variable. Add: rename walrus-bound variable, inline var defined by walrus, extract function with walrus in condition.

title: Add comprehension scope tests
description: Comprehension variables have their own scope in Python 3. Rename inner comprehension variable, extract from comprehension body, inline var used in comprehension. Test list, dict, set, and generator comprehensions.

title: Add except-as and exception handling scope tests
description: Python 3 implicitly deletes the except-as variable after the handler. Rename of except-as binding, extract from except body, inline involving exception vars. Also test except* (3.11+) if supported by parso.

title: Add async/await tests across refactoring operations
description: async def, await, async for, async with are untested. Rename of async functions, extract from async body, inline in async context. Extract function containing await should produce async def.
close_reason: Added async-function rename and async-await-bug extract_function tests

title: Add nonlocal/global declaration tests
description: nonlocal and global are untested in all 4 operations. Rename with nonlocal should update all scope references. Extract function with nonlocal must propagate the declaration. Inline involving global vars needs testing.

title: Add f-string tests across all refactoring operations

Extract variable currently errors on fstring_start (known bug jedi-czz). Test: rename var in f-string, inline var used in f-string, extract f-string as variable.

title: Expand refactoring test coverage for untested Python constructs
description: Systematic expansion of test coverage across all 4 refactoring operations (inline, extract_variable, extract_function, rename) for Python constructs that are currently untested. Based on gap analysis comparing jedi's tests against rope, JetBrains/PyCharm, and academic research.
close_reason: All 19 gap tests added and passing. Total test count now 169 (up from 150).

title: extract_variable walrus operator gives unhelpful error message
description: Extracting (y := 3) gives 'Cannot extract a namedexpr_test' which exposes parser internals. Should say something like 'Cannot extract a walrus/assignment expression'.
close_reason: Improved error messages: namedexpr_test→walrus operator, fstring_start→f-string

title: extract_variable cannot extract f-strings
description: Attempting to extract an f-string raises RefactoringError: Cannot extract a fstring_start. The fstring type is not in _VARIABLE_EXCTRACTABLE list. This is a limitation users may encounter.
close_reason: Fixed: extract_variable now handles f-strings by climbing from fstring_start/end to parent fstring node

title: Inline adds double parens around already-parenthesized expressions
description: When inlining a = (1 + 2) used as 'test(a * 3)', produces 'test(((1 + 2)) * 3)' instead of 'test((1 + 2) * 3)'. The outer parens of the rhs are included in replace_code and then another layer is added by the parens logic.
close_reason: Fixed: already-parenthesized expressions no longer double-wrapped during inline

title: Inline adds unnecessary parens around simple literals
description: When inlining x = 42 in 'return x + 1', produces 'return (42) + 1' instead of 'return 42 + 1'. The parens are added because tree_name.parent.type is in EXPRESSION_PARTS (arith_expr), but a simple literal doesn't need wrapping.
close_reason: Fixed: simple literals no longer wrapped in parens during inline

title: extract_function: match/case block extraction (Python 3.10+)
description:
There are no extract_function tests for `match`/`case` syntax (Python 3.10+).

Example gaps:
1. Extracting a return expression inside a `case` branch:
```python
def handle(cmd):
    match cmd:
        case 'quit':
            return do_quit()
        case 'go':
            return do_go()
```
2. Extracting a range that contains the entire `match` block.

The `match` statement introduces new AST node types (`match_stmt`, `case_clause`) not present in the existing tests. Verify that `_find_non_global_names` correctly traverses `match` nodes and that `_check_for_non_extractables` does not break on `match`/`case` keywords.

title: extract_function: multiple context managers in with statement
description:
The test `with-statement-range` covers extraction from inside a `with` statement with a single context manager. There is no test for extracting from a `with` statement that has multiple context managers.

Example gap:
```python
def f():
    with open('a') as r, open('b', 'w') as w:
        data = r.read()
        w.write(data)
```
Extracting the body of the `with` statement — the extracted function should receive both `r` and `w` as parameters (they are used but not defined in the extracted range). This tests whether `_find_inputs_and_outputs` correctly identifies both `with` targets as inputs.

title: extract_function: range spanning try+except blocks together
description:
The test `with-try-except` covers extraction from *inside* an `except` clause. There is no test for extracting a range that spans both the `try` block and the `except` block together.

Example gap:
```python
def f(data):
    try:
        x = parse(data)
    except ValueError:
        x = default()
    return x
```
Extracting the entire `try/except` range — the extracted function should handle the `try/except` logic and return `x`. This tests the range-extraction code path with compound statements that have multiple branches.

title: extract_function: extracting range that writes a nonlocal variable
description:
No test for extracting a range that modifies a variable declared as `nonlocal` in the enclosing function.

Example gap:
```python
def outer():
    count = 0
    def inner():
        nonlocal count
        count += 1   # extracted range
        return count
```
When the range `count += 1` is extracted, the extracted function receives `count` as a parameter and returns the updated value — but the `nonlocal count` declaration inside `inner` means the original code modifies the outer scope in-place, while the extracted version breaks that contract.

The current test `nonlocal-read` only covers reading a nonlocal variable (not writing). This gap tests the write case, which involves the `nonlocal` declaration and augmented assignment.

title: extract_function: range containing bare raise re-raises outside active exception
description:
No test for extracting a range that contains a bare `raise` statement inside a `try/except` block.

Example gap:
```python
def f():
    try:
        risky()
    except Exception as e:
        log(e)
        raise   # bare re-raise
```
If the range includes the `raise` statement, the extracted function would contain a bare `raise` but there may be no active exception when it's called. The tool should either:
1. Error with a `RefactoringError` explaining the bare re-raise issue, OR
2. Allow it and let the user handle the semantics

There is currently no test verifying which behavior occurs. The `_check_for_non_extractables` function in extract.py only guards against `return` and `yield` — `raise` is not guarded.

title: extract_function: multiple stacked decorators on source function
extract_function: extraction from class body with only pass
description:
The tests `in-class-1` and `in-class-range-1` cover extraction from a class body that has multiple statements. There is no test for extracting from a class body whose body is only a `pass` statement or a class body that has a single expression statement.

Example gap:
```python
class Empty:
    pass
    x = compute()  # extracted line
```
Or more practically:
```python
class Foo:
    result = expensive_computation(a, b)
```
Extracting `result = expensive_computation(a, b)` from a class that has no other methods — the new function is inserted before the class definition. Verify the blank-line handling and indentation are correct.

title: extract_function: yield from rejection
description:
The tests `random-yield-1` and `random-yield-2` confirm extraction is rejected when `yield` appears in the range. However, there is no test for `yield from` expressions.

In parso, `yield from expr` is a `yield_expr` node containing a `yield` keyword followed by `from` and the expression. The `_check_for_non_extractables` function in extract.py checks for a leaf with `value == 'yield'`, which should catch this — but it is not verified by a test.

Add a test that tries to extract a range containing a `yield from` statement from a generator function and confirms the expected `RefactoringError: Cannot extract yield statements.` is raised.

title: extract_function: multiple return variables (tuple-return extraction)
description:
No test for extracting a range where multiple variables are assigned and then both used after the extracted range. The extracted function needs to `return x, y` and the call site needs tuple unpacking.

Example gap:
```python
def f():
    x, y = compute()
    return x + y
```
Extracting the range `x, y = compute()` — the extracted function should:
- accept the needed inputs as parameters
- `return x, y` (multiple return values)
- The call site should unpack: `x, y = extracted()`

This exercises the code path in extract.py where `return_variables` contains more than one element and `output_var_str = ', '.join(return_variables)` produces a tuple-return.

title: introduce_field: variable with inline comment on assignment line
description:
No test covers introduce_field when the assignment line has a trailing comment, e.g.:

    def foo(self):
        x = 42  # important value
        return x

After introduce_field, the comment should be preserved on the 'self.x = 42  # important value' line and not dropped or duplicated.

title: introduce_field: deeply nested class (class inside class)
extract_function: async for / async with range extraction
description:
No test for extracting a range that contains an `async for` or `async with` body. The extracted function must be declared `async def` because it contains async iteration/context-manager syntax.

The `_contains_await` check in extract.py (line 277) only looks for the `await` keyword leaf, NOT for `async for`/`async with` keywords. This means ranges with `async for` or `async with` may be incorrectly emitted as plain `def` instead of `async def`.

Example gaps to test:
1. Range extraction spanning an `async for` loop body inside an `async def`

No test verifies that introduce_field correctly uses cls.x (not self.x) in these special class hooks, or provides an appropriate error if the semantics differ.

title: introduce_field: variable used in try/except blocks

title: introduce_parameter: positional-only separator /

title: introduce_parameter: bare * separator (keyword-only existing params)
